s.g: Pertaining to a diocese.
The bishop of a diocese.
An inhabitant of a diocese.
(historical) An administrative division of the later Roman Empire, established by the Herodian tetrarchy.
(Christianity) An ecclesiastical territory administered by a bishop.
Of or relating to the Roman emperor Diocletian.
(organic chemistry, in combination) Two octyl groups in a molecule
(electronics) An electronic device that allows current to flow in one direction only; used chiefly as a rectifier.
(botany) Having the male and female reproductive organs on separate plants (of the same species) rather than different parts of the same plant.
(zoology, rare) Having two distinct sexes.
(organic chemistry) any organic compound having two hydroxy functional groups
(organic chemistry, sometimes in combination) diketone
The orgiastic Ancient Greek festivals seasonally held in honor of Dionysus, which evolved into Greek comedy and tragedy.
(historical) Any of the ancient festivals held in honour of the Olympian god Dionysus, and corresponding to the Roman Bacchanalia.
s.x: The greater Dionysia were held at Athens in March or April, and were celebrated with elaborate performances of tragedies and comedies.

s.g: Of, or relating to Dionysus or to the Dionysia.
wild and ecstatic
Of or pertaining to Dionysus.
A follower of Dionysus.
One who is dionysian.
Wild, irrational, undisciplined, orgiastic.
(mathematics) Of or pertaining to Diophantus, the Greek mathematician.
(mineralogy) A monoclinic pyroxene mineral, a magnesium calcium silicate with the chemical formula CaMgSi₂O₆, found in igneous and metamorphic rocks.
A unit of measure of the power of a lens or mirror, equal to the reciprocal of its focal length in meters. Myopia is diagnosed and measured in diopters.
The dioptre adjustment mechanism of a pair of binoculars or of a camera viewfinder.
(photography, dated) A lens element attached to the front of a photographic lens to shorten the lens's minimum focus distance; also called a "close-up filter".
(obsolete) Any lens system, such as a telescope.
(obsolete) A theodolite or similar surveyor’s angle measuring device.
Acting as a medium for sight; making use of refraction (of lenses, etc.).
(obsolete) Pertaining to a diopter.
(obsolete) Capable of being seen through.
(in the plural) The branch of optics concerned with refraction.
A dioptric telescope.
A three-dimensional display of a scenery, often having a painted background in front of which models are arranged, e.g. in a museum where stuffed animals are presented against a painted landscape.
(geology) A grey intrusive igneous rock composed mostly of plagioclase feldspar, biotite, hornblende and/or pyroxene.

dios.f: Abbreviation of distal intestinal obstruction syndrome.

s.g: A monosaccharide containing two carbon atoms.
Any tree of the genus Diospyros.
(chemistry) Any of a class of six-membered, saturated heterocycles having four carbon atoms and two oxygen atoms in the ring.
(chemistry) Any oxide containing two oxygen atoms in each molecule.
(countable, organic chemistry) The unsaturated six-membered heterocycle having four carbon atoms, two oxygen atoms, and two double bonds (molecular formula C₄H₄O₂); 1,2-dioxin and 1,4-dioxin.

(countable, organic chemistry) The parent compound dibenzo-1,4-dioxin or dibenzo-p-dioxin (molecular formula C₁₂H₈O₂), in which two benzene rings are connected through two oxygen atoms; dibenzodioxin, oxanthrene.
(countable, organic chemistry) Any of a broad range of toxic or carcinogenic halogenated polycyclic compounds that occur as byproducts of herbicides.

(uncountable, specifically, loosely) The compound 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD; molecular formula C₁₂H₄Cl₄O₂), a persistent organic pollutant of the environment which is generally produced as a byproduct of organic synthesis or when organic materials are burned.
(inorganic chemistry) Diatomic oxygen: the normal allotrope of oxygen, having two atoms per molecule.
(inorganic chemistry, in combination) Two atoms of oxygen in a molecule.
(biochemistry) Any of several enzymes that catalyze dioxygenation reactions
